questions.prompt: How does Anthropic's Building effective agents post separate workflows from agents?

options.text: Workflows follow set code paths; agents direct their own process and tools.
options.explanation: Right. The post says workflows give predictability for well-defined tasks, and agents give flexibility.

options.text: Workflows use small, cheap models; agents use large and costly models today.
options.explanation: The post doesn't define them by model size.

options.text: Workflows need people at every single step; agents need no people at all.
options.explanation: The post says agents can pause for human feedback at checkpoints too.

questions.prompt: According to OpenAI's guide, when should a run pause for human review?

options.text: Before every single model call, so that people can see and approve each step.
options.explanation: The guide doesn't ask for this. It points review at sensitive actions.

options.text: Only after the final answer has already been sent to the customer in full.
options.explanation: Review after the action is too late to stop it.

options.text: Before side effects like cancellations, edits or other sensitive actions.
options.explanation: Right. The run pauses, a person or policy approves or rejects, and the same run continues.

questions.prompt: OpenAI's support-agent cookbook moves some work out of the main path. Which work?

options.text: The resolve-or-escalate decision, because it is the slowest of all steps.
options.explanation: The cookbook keeps that decision in the main path. It changes the outcome.

options.text: QA notes, tags, audits and reports that don't change the outcome.
options.explanation: Right. These can run as follow-up work after the customer gets a reply.

options.text: The customer reply, which can be sent on the next day in a batch.
options.explanation: The reply stays in the main path. Only work that doesn't change the outcome moves.
